notes.title: Chapter map: Structured output & control

headings.text: 🌳 How should this output be enforced?

notes.html:
How the output of a call is held to a contract that code can rely on. Note 35 frames it as layers with different guarantees; 36 chooses the provider mechanism; 37 covers your own grammar when a schema can't say it; 39 is what happens when an output still fails; 43 says what "the same answer every time" can and cannot mean; 38, 40, 41 and 42 are short notes on tool calls, length, prefill and classification. Read each arrow as a sentence: the layered contract is enforced first by a schema.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another section. Two yellow nodes hold two notes each.

Reading order:35 a layered contract36 JSON mode and schemas39 parse and repair37 your own grammar43 deterministic prompting42 classification38 tool calls40 output length41 prefill

Owners

Ideas several notes touch, and the one note that explains each. The first row's owner serves the whole pillar.

Idea Owner note
Validate → repair → fail: classify the failure, re-ask with the error, change a variable, bound by attempts and time, a visible fallback; count every repair 39 parse and repair
What a schema guarantee covers and where it stops (refusal, truncation, meaning); a strict consumer 35 a layered contract
Prompt-only vs JSON mode vs schema vs your own grammar; schema design for the enforcer; provider limits 36 JSON mode and schemas
When a grammar beats a schema; grammar count and cache as the cost; over-tight constraints 37 your own grammar
Temperature zero is not reproducibility; promise structure and decisions, log the rest 43 deterministic prompting
A token cap is a cut, not a length request 40 output length
What replaced each use of prefill 41 prefill
One-token labels, scores from logprobs, thresholds fitted on labelled data 42 classification
The three levels of a format; what each field means; reasoning field first output-format specification, not these notes
What prefill is and where it is supported system, user and prefill, not these notes
How a decoder masks tokens against a grammar structured and constrained decoding (LLM-Production), not these notes
Temperature, top-p and seeds as sampling mechanics decoding and sampling (LLM-Production), not these notes
Logprobs as a signal logprobs (LLM-Production), not these notes
Strict schemas for tool calls; what the model sees on a tool error structured output for tool calls and tool error handling (Agentic), not these notes
What a tool definition contains; how many tools; overlap tool schemas and tool design principles (Agentic), not these notes
Tool names and descriptions as prompt text tool descriptions as prompts, not these notes
JSON answers that carry sources structured output from RAG (RAG), not these notes
Retries, timeouts and circuit breakers as a platform concern reliability engineering, not these notes

Changed on 11 Oct 2026:

  • Note 37 moved from CORE to SUPPORTING. Its mechanism (compiling a grammar, masking tokens) is owned by the LLM-Production note; what stays is the decision to own a grammar and what that costs.
  • Note 38 moved from SUPPORTING to BREADTH and is now a pointer: its content was already owned by the Agentic tool notes and by note 58.
  • Note 41 stays BREADTH and no longer re-explains prefill; it lists what replaced each use.

The pillar now has 25 CORE, 64 SUPPORTING and 31 BREADTH notes. Older text of every note is in 08-Prompt-engineering/_superseded/04-Structured Output & Control/.

How should this output be enforced?

Every leaf except the first still ends in a validator you own and the repair policy of note 39.

  • ✍️ Instruction and example (19): if a later step starts parsing the text, go down the tree.
  • Enum (42): if you need a score to threshold, not only the label, read logprobs where the API offers them.
  • Your own grammar (37): if the output can be wrapped as a string field and checked by a parser after the call, a schema plus validation is less to own.
  • Schema-enforced (36): if the schema hits the provider's complexity limits, simplify the schema before leaving this leaf.
  • JSON mode with repair (39): if the model or provider gains schema enforcement, move up.

At a glance

Mechanism What it guarantees Extra cost per request Fails as What enforces it
Instruction in the prompt nothing tokens drift on long or odd inputs nothing: a request
JSON mode parseable JSON of any shape none the right syntax, the wrong keys the decoder (syntax only)
Schema-enforced output keys, types, enums a one-off compile per schema refusal; truncation; valid and wrong the decoder
Strict tool call tool name and argument shape as above the wrong tool chosen the decoder
Own grammar membership of any language you can write compile and memory per grammar perfect syntax around nonsense your decoder
Validator nothing; it detects negligible a rule you didn't write your code
Repair loop bounded behaviour on failure a round trip per attempt hides drift if uncounted your code
Temperature 0 greedy choice of token none still not identical runs nothing guarantees sameness
max_tokens a hard stop none a cut mid-object the server

Lineage

Year What appeared What it fixed Status
2020–22 "Reply in JSON" and regular expressions nothing reliably ⚪ Fading as the only layer
Jun 2023 Function calling in a provider API a typed way to ask for arguments 🟢 Established
Jul 2023 Efficient guided generation (the method behind Outlines) grammar enforcement cheap enough to serve 🟢 Established
Nov 2023 JSON mode prose wrapped around the JSON 🟡 a fallback now
Aug 2024 Schema-enforced structured output; the same month, a study of reasoning loss under strict formats wrong keys and types; and a warning about the price 🟢 Established
2024–25 Schema enforcement at the other major providers provider lock-in for this feature 🟢 Established
2025–26 Prefilled last turns rejected by newer Claude models — ⚪ prefill fading

Landscape (as of Oct 2026)

Read from each provider's page on 11 Oct 2026. The three differ in ways that leak into your schema, so an adapter per provider is normal.

Anthropic OpenAI Google (Gemini API)
Request output_config.format with type: "json_schema"; strict: true on a tool. Generally available. (output_format is deprecated) text.format with type: "json_schema", strict: true; JSON mode is type: "json_object" response_format with mime_type: application/json and a schema
Guarantee as stated "schema-compliant responses through constrained decoding" "only Structured Outputs ensure schema adherence"; JSON mode ensures valid JSON only "syntactically correct JSON"; "always validate values in your application"
When it does not hold stop_reason: "refusal"; stop_reason: "max_tokens"; enum values may differ in capitalisation a refusal item in place of the object; status: "incomplete" at the output-token limit not stated on the page read
Optional fields allowed, at most 24 across a request every field must be required; optional is a union with null not stated
Other limits 20 strict tools; 16 union-typed parameters; no recursion; no numeric or string-length constraints; additionalProperties must be false; "Schema is too complex" is a 400 root must be an object; additionalProperties: false; up to 5,000 properties and 10 levels; 1,000 enum values; recursion supported; allOf, not, if/then/else unsupported "a subset of the JSON Schema specification"; large or deeply nested schemas "may be rejected"
Key order in the output required properties first, then optional the order of keys in the schema not stated
First use of a schema extra latency while the grammar compiles; cached 24 hours from last use extra latency on the first request not stated
Does not combine with citations (400 error); message prefill — —
Also the grammar applies to the final output only, not to thinking, so the model can reason first; changing the format invalidates the prompt cache for the thread JSON mode errors unless the word "JSON" appears in the context with Gemini 3, structured output can be combined with built-in tools (preview)
Source structured outputs structured outputs structured output

Not re-read in this pass: logprob availability per provider, seed parameters, and the self-hosted libraries (Outlines, llama.cpp grammars, vLLM reproducibility modes). Notes 37, 42 and 43 state those durably and link the docs.

Four bullets

  • The one big idea: the prompt asks for a shape, the decoder can guarantee the shape, and nothing guarantees the meaning. So every structured output needs three things you own: a validator for meaning, a policy for the outputs that fail, and a counter on both.
  • The two most-confused pairs: JSON mode vs a schema (36: parseable, against your keys and types) · a re-ask vs a retry (39: the error is fed back, against the same request sent again).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: note 39's ladder and failure-class table, note 36's mechanism table and the two exits (refusal, truncation), note 35's "valid is not correct" example, note 43's guarantee table.
  • Cross-section links: the prompt half of the contract is output-format specification; the tool-call version is the Agentic note on structured output for tool calls; the platform-level retry and fallback design is reliability engineering. Content gaps: none in this section.

notes.title: Structured Output Is a Systems Problem — A Guarantee of Shape Is Not a Guarantee of Meaning
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: structured outputs · OpenAI: structured outputs · Tam et al. 2024: Let Me Speak Freely? · Instructor: structured LLM outputs

TL;DR

Getting reliable structured output is not about phrasing. The contract runs through four layers: the prompt asks, the decoder guarantees the shape, your validator checks the meaning, your policy decides what happens on failure. Only one layer gives a guarantee, and it guarantees shape only: a valid object can hold a made-up id. The design question is where each failure goes, and what the consuming code does when the contract breaks.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:prompt asks for the objectschema-enforced decoding ─refusal or cut-off: no objectrepair policy
your validator (ranges, ids, cross-field sums)repair policystrict consumer

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four layers? Prompt instruction, schema-enforced decoding, your validator, a repair and fallback policy.
What does a shape guarantee not give? Meaning: a valid object can hold an invented id or a negative amount.
Two ways the shape guarantee itself fails? A refusal, and output cut off at the token limit.

The idea

An invoice extractor uses the provider's schema enforcement. Every response parses. Finance later finds an invoice whose cited_clause quotes a sentence that is not in the source document, and another with a total of −40.

Nothing malfunctioned. The schema said cited_clause is a string and total is a number, and both were. A schema describes types and structure. It cannot know that the string must appear in a particular document, or that this number can't be negative for your business.

So treat the output as passing through layers, each with a different strength. The prompt asks, and usually gets. The decoder, when schema enforcement is on, makes a malformed object impossible. Your validator checks what only you know. And a policy decides what happens to whatever fails: retry, escalate, or hand to a person.

Two exits bypass the decoder's guarantee altogether, and the provider documents both: the model may refuse, and generation may hit the token limit mid-object.

The trade: each layer you add catches a class of failure the one before can't, and each is one more thing to build, count and keep in step.

How it works

Where each layer stands, and what gets past it.

Layer Guarantees Lets through Enforced by
Prompt instruction nothing anything, rarely nothing: a request
Schema-enforced decoding keys, types, enums a refusal; a cut-off; valid and wrong values the provider's decoder
Your validator nothing; it detects rules you didn't write your code
Repair and fallback policy bounded behaviour — your code
Rule What actually happens
Syntax down, meaning up Put shape in the decoder, the only layer that can guarantee it. Put meaning in a validator you own, because only you know the rules.
Decide the consumer's behaviour A tolerant consumer that fills defaults turns a measurable failure into silence. A strict one makes it loud, and then needs the policy behind it.
Read the stop reason before parsing A refusal and a cut-off both look like "bad output" to a parser and need opposite handling.

Evolution

Lineage:2020–22 one layer: ask, then regex2023 JSON mode: syntax onlyAug 2024 schema enforcement: shape guaranteed2024–25 validation libraries make re-asking routine
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Stronger models make the prompt layer and the validator fail less often. What won't change: no provider can check a value against your documents or your business rules, and a refusal or a cut-off is never a valid object.

Code

The checks a schema cannot express, run on an object that already has a valid shape.

def validate(inv: dict, source: str, order_total: float) -> list[str]:
    errors = []
    if inv["total"] < 0 or inv["total"] > order_total:
        errors.append("total out of range")                       # a number, but not a sane one
    if inv["cited_clause"] not in source:
        errors.append("cited_clause not found in the document")   # a string, but invented
    if abs(sum(i["amount"] for i in inv["lines"]) - inv["total"]) > 0.01:
        errors.append("lines do not add up to total")             # each field fine, together wrong
    return errors

doc = "Payment is due within 30 days of delivery."
obj = {"total": -40.0, "cited_clause": "Payment is due within 14 days.", "lines": [{"amount": -40.0}]}
print(validate(obj, doc, order_total=500.0))
# → ['total out of range', 'cited_clause not found in the document']
# look for: two errors on an object that any schema check would pass
# naive belief predicts: an empty list, because the object is schema-valid

Run on Python 3.9, it prints those two errors.

Measure it

  • Offline: per-rule validator failure rate on the golden set, with schema enforcement on. This is the error the shape guarantee hides.
  • In production: counts per layer and cause: refusals, cut-offs, validator failures by rule, repairs, fallbacks. One merged "parse error" number cannot be acted on.
  • Enforced by: the decoder for shape; your validator and a strict consumer for everything else. The prompt layer is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: Structured output looks like a prompting problem and isn't. The contract spans four layers: an instruction in the prompt, a decoder constraint that guarantees syntax, a validator for meaning, and a policy for failures. Only the second gives a guarantee, and it covers shape: schema-valid JSON with a fabricated id parses perfectly. So I design where each layer's failures go and what the consumer does when the contract breaks.

Q · Mechanism — If the provider guarantees schema conformance, what is left to engineer? Two things. Meaning: the schema says a citation id is a string, not that it names a document that was actually retrieved, so every field that refers to the real world needs my own check. The exits: a refusal or hitting the token limit produces output that doesn't match the schema, so the non-conforming branch must exist.

Q · Trade-off — Where do you put the strictness: decoder, validator or consumer? The simpler rung is one layer, an instruction and a tolerant parser, which is fine while prototyping. For a consumer that is code, I push syntax into the decoder, meaning into a validator I own, and make the consumer strict with a bounded repair ladder and a visible fallback behind it. A tolerant consumer is the dangerous choice: the violation rate reads zero while quality drifts. And on reasoning-heavy tasks I loosen the decoder and tighten the validator.

Pitfalls

  • "Schema-enforced output means the output is correct"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "guaranteed" is the word in the documentation.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the guarantee is about form. A valid object can carry a fabricated citation, a negative amount, or an enum value that names the wrong category.
    ↳ Think instead: valid means well-formed; correct needs a check you write.
  • "A forgiving parser is defensive engineering"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it keeps the pipeline running through bad outputs.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it hides regressions. My repair path absorbed a growing share of responses and reported success while the real format-failure rate climbed.
    ↳ Think instead: a repair that isn't counted is a failure you agreed not to see.
  • Not the same: a parse failure vs a refusal vs a cut-off
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: all three arrive as "the object isn't there".
    ↳ Difference: a parse failure may be worth a re-ask. A refusal must not be retried. A cut-off needs a larger token limit or a smaller request.
    ↳ Think instead: branch on the stop reason first, then parse.
  • Don't build four layers for output a person reads.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: strictness feels like quality.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a schema on a chat reply makes it stiffer and buys nothing; people tolerate variation that code can't.
    ↳ Do instead: scale strictness with how mechanical the consumer is.
  • Shelf life: "shape is not meaning" is durable. Which exits exist, and the limits on schemas, are provider facts that change.

Connections

Path:output-format specificationa layered contractJSON mode and schemasparsing and repair loops
  • Builds on failure taxonomy: format drift is the class fixed outside the prompt.
  • Enforced by parsing and repair loops: the policy layer.
  • Owned elsewhere: structured output from RAG covers objects that carry sources.
  • Measured by assertion-based testing: the validator's rules as tests.
  • Drilled in JSON mode, schema or repair.

notes.title: JSON Mode & Schema-Enforced Output — What Each Provider Mechanism Guarantees
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: structured outputs · OpenAI: structured outputs · Gemini API: structured output · OpenAI: introducing Structured Outputs in the API · Tam et al. 2024: Let Me Speak Freely?

TL;DR

Three provider mechanisms, three strengths. Prompt only: nothing is guaranteed. JSON mode: the output parses as JSON, of any shape. Schema-enforced output: the output matches your keys, types and enums, because the decoder can't emit anything else. The schema guarantee stops at two exits, a refusal and a token-limit cut-off, and never covers meaning. The schema you send is also not plain JSON Schema: each provider accepts a subset, and the subsets differ.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:your schemaprovider compiles it to a grammar (first use is slower, then cached)decoding can only follow the grammarstop reasonno valid object
valid shapeyour validator

Recall

Prompt Answer
JSON mode vs schema-enforced? Valid JSON of any shape, vs valid JSON matching your schema.
Two ways the schema guarantee fails? A refusal, and a cut-off at the token limit.
What does the first request with a new schema cost? Extra latency to compile the grammar; cached afterwards.
What is never guaranteed? That the values are true, in range or drawn from the source.
Why can't one schema go to every provider? Each supports a different subset of JSON Schema.
Draw by hand: the path of a schema Schema → compile and cache → constrained decoding → two exits (refusal, cut-off) → validator.

The idea

A team asks for JSON in the prompt and gets it almost always. They switch on JSON mode to remove "almost". The next failure is a response that parses perfectly: {"result": "I could not find an invoice number"}. Their code wanted five named fields and crashes on a missing key.

JSON mode solved one problem: prose around the JSON. It promises that the text parses, and nothing about what is inside.

Schema-enforced output is the stronger mechanism. You send a JSON Schema; the provider compiles it into a grammar; during generation, any token that would break the grammar is removed from the choices. A missing required field or a wrong type is not unlikely, it is unreachable. This is the first layer in the pillar that is enforced, not requested.

Then read the small print, because the guarantee is narrow. It is about shape. It does not apply when the model refuses or when the output is cut off at the token limit. And the schema must fit the provider's rules: one requires every field to be listed as required, another caps optional fields and forbids numeric ranges.

The trade: schema enforcement removes malformed output for the price of a schema written to a provider's subset, a compile on first use, and possible loss of reasoning quality if the format leaves no room to think.

How it works

What happens to your schema, and where the guarantee holds.

The two red exits are documented by the providers; code must handle both before it parses anything.

Rule What actually happens
Write the schema for the enforcer Limits you can't express (a minimum, a string length) go into the field's description and into your validator. Anthropic's SDK helpers do this move for you.
Prefer closed sets An enum is enforced by the decoder; a free string is not. On Anthropic, compare enum values case-insensitively.
Give reasoning room Put a reasoning field first, or let the model think before the constrained answer: on Anthropic the grammar applies to the final output only, not to thinking.
Few schemas, reused Compilation is per schema. A service with five schemas pays it five times; one with a schema per tenant pays it constantly.
Flatten before you fight a limit "Schema is too complex" is a signal to simplify: fewer optional and union-typed fields, less nesting.

How the decoder masks tokens is owned by structured and constrained decoding. What the prompt should say about each field is output-format specification.

Evolution

Lineage:2020–22 "reply in JSON"Jun 2023 function calling as a typed channelNov 2023 JSON modeAug 2024 schema-enforced structured output2024–25 the other major providers follow; SDK helpers take a typed class as the schema
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): generally available at the providers read for this note.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Newer models match a described schema reliably without enforcement; Anthropic's guide suggests trying that first, with retries. What won't change: only the decoder can make a malformed object impossible, and no decoder knows whether a value is true.
  • Checked on: provider rules read 11 Oct 2026.

Code

Schema-enforced extraction with both exits handled.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Invoice(BaseModel):
    reasoning: str                      # ① first: room to think before deciding
    total: float = Field(ge=0)          # ② ge=0 is OUR check; the grammar guarantees a number, not a sane one
    currency: str
    cited_clause: str                   # must appear word for word in the source

MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"             # as of Oct 2026

def extract(doc: str, client) -> Invoice | None:
    r = client.messages.parse(model=MODEL, max_tokens=2048, output_format=Invoice,
                              messages=[{"role": "user", "content": doc}])
    if r.stop_reason in ("refusal", "max_tokens"):      # ③ the two exits: never assume a valid object
        metrics.incr(f"nonconforming.{r.stop_reason}")
        return None
    out = r.parsed_output
    if out.cited_clause not in doc:                     # ④ meaning: a check the provider can't do
        metrics.incr("cited_clause_not_in_source")
        return None
    return out

Break it: the belief that a correct JSON Schema can be sent to any provider as it is.

schema = {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": False, "required": ["total"],
          "properties": {"total": {"type": "number", "minimum": 0}, "note": {"type": "string", "maxLength": 80}}}
def lint(s):
    props, issues = s["properties"], []
    for name, p in props.items():
        for k in ("minimum", "maximum", "minLength", "maxLength"):
            if k in p: issues.append(f"{name}.{k}: not enforced by Anthropic's grammar")
        if name not in s["required"]: issues.append(f"{name}: optional, but OpenAI requires every field")
    return issues
print(*lint(schema), sep="\n")
# look for: three issues on a schema that is valid JSON Schema
# naive belief predicts: none

Run on Python 3.9, it prints total.minimum, note.maxLength and note: optional. The rules are the providers' as read on 11 Oct 2026; an adapter per provider rewrites the schema, and your validator keeps the limits the grammar dropped.

Measure it

  • Offline: on the golden set, validator failure rate by rule with enforcement on, and task accuracy with enforcement on against off: the second number is what the format costs.
  • In production: stop-reason distribution per route (a rising cut-off rate is an input-length problem, not a format one), schema-compile latency on first use, and any route that still answers without a schema.
  • Enforced by: the provider's decoder, for shape. Your validator, for meaning. The two exits are handled by your code or not at all.

Interview

30-second answer: Provider structured-output features compile my JSON Schema into a grammar and constrain decoding, so the response conforms by construction. That's a step change from asking in the prompt. But the guarantee is narrow: shape, not meaning; it doesn't hold on a refusal or a token-limit cut-off; schemas must fit a provider-specific subset; and the first request compiles. JSON mode is weaker still: valid JSON of any shape.

Q · Mechanism — What is the difference between JSON mode and schema-enforced output? JSON mode guarantees the response parses as JSON and nothing about its shape, so I can get {"result": "not sure"} when I asked for five fields. It fixed prose-wrapped JSON and no more. Schema-enforced output compiles my schema into a grammar that masks tokens during decoding: required fields are present, types match, enum values come from my list. The same machinery sits behind strict tool calls, which is why the two share limits.

Q · Trade-off — The provider's feature, or your own grammar with a library? The simpler rung is the provider's feature, and I take it by default: nothing to host, kept in step with the model, and it covers JSON Schema, which is what nearly all outputs need. I'd own a grammar for something a schema can't express, a query language or a strict string pattern, or when I host the model anyway. Hitting the provider's complexity limits is usually a reason to simplify the schema. That case is your own grammar.

Q · Failure — Schema enforcement is on and production still shows parse failures. First the two documented exits. Cut-offs: the guarantee covers what is emitted, not an object truncated at the token limit, and it correlates with input length. Refusals: not schema-shaped. Then a path that never used the feature: a fallback model, a streaming path, a batch job. Then consumers that assume key order or exact enum casing. I'd confirm by logging the raw response with route, input length and stop reason on every failure.

Q · Design — An extraction service across two providers, feeding billing. Billing makes a wrong-but-valid object worse than a failure, so validation of meaning is mandatory and the same for both providers. One canonical schema lives in my code; an adapter per provider translates it to that provider's subset and normalises the response, including key order and enum case. Every response then passes one validation stage, and failures go to a bounded repair ladder and a review queue, never a default. I'd watch validator failures by provider and rule first. The layers are in the prompt-layer reference architecture.

Compare

Mechanism Guarantees Does not hold when Use when
Prompt only nothing inputs are long, odd or hostile prototyping; a person reads the output
JSON mode parseable JSON the keys are wrong but it parses the shape is free-form; no schema support
Schema-enforced output keys, types, enums refusal; cut-off code consumes the output: the default
Strict tool call tool name and argument shape same exits; the wrong tool chosen the output is an action
Your own grammar any language you can write you own its speed and edge cases a non-JSON language; self-hosted models

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Schema adherence 100% with enforcement, under 40% without OpenAI's own eval of complex schema following: gpt-4o-2024-08-06 with Structured Outputs against gpt-4-0613 prompted, 2024 cited (vendor): OpenAI announcement
Grammar cache 24 hours from last use Anthropic cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)
Limits per request 20 strict tools, 24 optional parameters, 16 union-typed parameters Anthropic cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: JSON mode vs a schema
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are switches described as "returns JSON".
    ↳ Difference: JSON mode guarantees the text parses. A schema guarantees your keys, types and enums.
    ↳ Think instead: if code reads named fields, JSON mode is not enough.
  • "With structured output on, parsing can't fail, so the error branch is dead code"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the feature is described as a guarantee.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a refusal and a token-limit cut-off both return something that is not your object, by design. That branch fires on your longest and most sensitive inputs.
    ↳ Think instead: guaranteed, unless it refuses or is cut off.
  • "The schema is the contract, so if it validates, downstream is safe"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the schema is the most precise description of the output there is.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it types a citation as a string and says nothing about whether the string is in the source. The substring check I added later caught more real errors than the schema did.
    ↳ Think instead: the schema is the contract for shape; the validator is the contract for meaning.
  • "Schema constraints are free"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: they only remove invalid tokens.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: there is a compile on first use, hard complexity limits, and published evidence that strict formats can lower reasoning quality.
    ↳ Think instead: budget for the compile, design for the limits, leave room to reason.
  • Don't design around features that don't combine.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: each feature works in isolation in a prototype.
    ↳ What goes wrong: on Anthropic, structured output with citations returns an error, and changing the output format invalidates the prompt cache for that thread.
    ↳ Do instead: check the provider's compatibility list before committing to a design that needs both.
  • Don't reach for your own grammar to emit plain JSON.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a library gives full control.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you rebuild a managed feature and own its performance.
    ↳ Do instead: use the provider's feature and justify the exception.
  • Shelf life: the three strengths and the two exits are durable. Parameter names, limits and schema subsets changed within the past year and will again.

Connections

Path:a layered contractJSON mode and schemasparsing and repair loopsyour own grammar
  • Builds on output-format specification: the prompt's half of the contract.
  • Owned elsewhere: structured and constrained decoding (LLM-Production) covers the mechanism; structured output for tool calls (Agentic) covers strict tool arguments.
  • Enforced by parsing and repair loops: what handles the two exits.
  • Breaks when combined with prompt caching if the format changes mid-thread.
  • Measured by assertion-based testing: validator rules as tests.
  • Drilled in JSON mode, schema or repair.

notes.title: Your Own Grammar — When a Schema Can't Say It, and What Owning the Decoder Costs
notes.html:
References

Willard & Louf 2023: Efficient Guided Generation for LLMs · Outlines: grammar-structured generation · llama.cpp: grammars · Tam et al. 2024: Let Me Speak Freely?

TL;DR

A provider's schema feature enforces JSON Schema. Some outputs are not JSON objects: a query language, a config format, a string that must match a pattern. For those you supply a grammar and run the constrained decoder yourself. The guarantee is the same kind, and just as narrow: the output is in the language. It may still be wrong, unauthorised or absurd. What you take on is cost per distinct grammar: compiling, caching and memory.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:language definition + current field namesgrammar ─compile once per version, cacheconstrained generationoutput is always in the languagechecks after decoding: permission, costrun it

Recall

Prompt Answer
When do you need your own grammar? The output is a language JSON Schema can't describe, or you host the model yourself.
What does it guarantee? Membership of the language; nothing about truth, permission or sense.
Where is the cost? Per distinct grammar: compile time and cached memory, not per token.

The idea

A product turns "orders over £500 from Germany last month" into a filter expression: country = "DE" AND total > 500 AND date >= 2026-09-01. With a schema you can say "the answer is a string". You cannot say "the string has balanced brackets, known field names and valid operators". One request in fifty comes back with a field that doesn't exist.

That requirement is a grammar, written by you for your own language. A constrained decoder then allows, at each step, only tokens that can continue a valid expression. Put the current field names into the grammar as its vocabulary and a non-existent field can't be written at all.

How the masking works is owned by the LLM-Production note; here the question is whether to own it.

Owning it means the model runs where you control decoding, and it means paying per grammar. Each grammar is compiled into a lookup over the whole vocabulary, once, then reused. One grammar reused a million times is nearly free; a grammar per tenant is compiled on the request path again and again.

The trade: a grammar makes invalid syntax impossible for languages no schema can describe, and makes you the owner of a decoder's speed, memory and edge cases.

How it works

What the grammar closes, and what stays open.

Check Closed by the grammar? Where it is handled
balanced brackets, valid operators yes the decoder
only field names that exist yes, if the names are in the grammar the decoder, per schema version
this caller may filter on that field no a check after decoding
the query is cheap enough to run no a cost estimate after decoding
Rule What actually happens
Count your grammars Cache by schema version, not by tenant. "A schema per tenant" is usually one grammar with tenant-specific values checked afterwards.
Characters and tokens don't line up A grammar is written over characters; the model emits tokens that span several. Whitespace and Unicode are where a correct-looking grammar rejects valid text.
Too tight produces nonsense If only tokens the model finds very unlikely are allowed, it must still pick one. The result is valid syntax around gibberish, which is harder to notice than a parse error.

Evolution

Lineage:Jul 2023 efficient guided generation: indexing makes it cheap per token2023–24 libraries for regular expressions, schemas and full grammarsAug 2024 providers ship the JSON Schema case as a feature
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026) as a technique.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. A strong model writes a small language correctly almost always, and a parser after the call catches the rest. What won't change: "almost always" is not "always", and where an invalid output is unacceptable only the decoder closes the gap.

Code

The grammar is keyed by schema version; permission is checked after decoding.

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=64)                              # ① cache on the schema VERSION, never per tenant
def generator(schema_version: str):
    grammar = build_filter_grammar(registry.fields(schema_version))   # field names become the grammar's vocabulary
    return compile_grammar(MODEL, grammar)          # the expensive step: done once per version

def to_filter(question: str, schema_version: str, caller) -> str:
    q = generator(schema_version)(PROMPT.format(question=question))   # ② cannot be syntactically invalid
    denied = [f for f in fields_in(q) if not caller.may_filter(f)]
    if denied:                                      # ③ well-formed and not allowed: the grammar can't know
        metrics.incr("filter.permission_denied")
        raise PermissionError(denied)
    return q

compile_grammar stands for the library call (Outlines, a llama.cpp grammar, a server's guided-decoding option); interfaces differ by version.

Measure it

  • Offline: share of outputs that are valid and also pass the permission and cost checks, against a schema-typed string with a parser after the call.
  • In production: grammar-cache hit rate and compile time at the 95th percentile; rejections after decoding, split by cause.
  • Enforced by: your decoder, for syntax. Your checks after decoding, for permission and cost. Meaning is not enforced.

Interview

30-second answer: Provider schema features cover JSON. When the output is a language, a filter expression or a query, I supply a grammar and constrain decoding myself, so invalid syntax is unreachable. The guarantee is membership of the language and nothing more, so permission and cost are checked after decoding. The production question isn't masking speed, it's how many distinct grammars I have and whether they stay cached.

Q · Mechanism — Why isn't checking a grammar at every token far too slow? Because nothing is checked per token. The grammar is compiled into a state machine, and for each state the set of vocabulary tokens that may come next is precomputed. At generation time the work is a lookup, a mask and a transition. The cost moved to compilation, done once per grammar and cached.

Q · Trade-off — Where does constrained decoding stop being the right tool? The simpler rung is a schema-typed string plus a parser and a re-ask, and with a strong model that is often enough. I own a grammar when invalid output is unacceptable and the language is beyond a schema. Two limits remain. Masking changes the distribution, so forcing an answer before any reasoning can lower quality: leave a free field or a separate call for the thinking.

Pitfalls

  • "Constrained decoding forces the right answer"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: invalid output really does become impossible.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it forces membership of a language. Inside that language the model can write a valid query that returns nothing, or one that reads a table it shouldn't.
    ↳ Think instead: it removes one kind of failure, malformed output, and no others.
  • "Grammar checking at every token must dominate the cost"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a parser running thousands of times sounds expensive.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: indexing moves nearly all the work to compile time. I worried about per-step cost when the real latency problem was grammar diversity and cache misses.
    ↳ Think instead: the cost is per distinct grammar, not per token.
  • Not the same: a grammar vs a schema
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: a provider turns your schema into a grammar, so they sound like one thing.
    ↳ Difference: a schema describes a JSON object's keys and types. A grammar can describe any language, including ones with nesting and operators that no schema covers.
    ↳ Think instead: if the output is an object, use a schema; if it is a language, you need a grammar.
  • Don't compile a grammar per tenant or per request.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: each tenant's fields differ, so a grammar each feels natural.
    ↳ What goes wrong: compilation never pays back; cold tenants wait, and thousands of cached grammars eat memory.
    ↳ Do instead: group tenants into a few grammar families, warm them at deploy, and check tenant-specific values after decoding.
  • Shelf life: "in the language is not correct" and "count your grammars" are durable. Library interfaces and how much a provider's schema subset can express both move.

Connections

Path:JSON mode and schemasyour own grammarparsing and repair loopsdeterministic prompting
  • Builds on JSON mode and schemas: the default this is the exception to.
  • Owned elsewhere: structured and constrained decoding (LLM-Production) covers compiling and masking.
  • Enforced by defence in depth: permission checks sit outside the model.
  • Costed in latency budget: cold-grammar compiles on the request path.

notes.title: Function & Tool-Call Prompting — A Tool Definition Is Prompt Text With a Schema Attached
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: structured outputs (strict tool use) · OpenAI: function calling

TL;DR

A tool call is structured output with a name. Strict mode guarantees the call is well-formed; it does not decide whether calling that tool was right. Most failures are the wrong tool, not wrong arguments. This note is a pointer.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
Where is the "prompt" in a tool? Its name, description and parameter descriptions, read on every turn.
What does strict mode guarantee? The tool name and argument shape. Not the choice of tool.
A tool as an output format? One tool with an enum field is a way to get a closed label.

The idea

Two tools, search_orders and lookup_order, with overlapping descriptions are confused on every ambiguous request, however strict the argument schema. The fix is in the text and the tool count.

If you want to know… Read
how names and descriptions steer the choice tool descriptions as prompts
what a definition contains tool schemas
how many tools, and overlap tool design principles
what strict arguments buy in a loop structured output for tool calls (Agentic)

One use belongs here: a single tool with one enum parameter is a common way to force a closed label. Anthropic's guide (Oct 2026) recommends it, or structured outputs, for classification.

Evolution

Lineage:Jun 2023 function callingAug 2024 strict argument schemas. 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): on Anthropic, strict tools and schema-enforced responses can be used in one request, with at most 20 strict tools.

notes.title: Parsing & Repair Loops — Classify the Failure, Feed the Error Back, Fail Where It Shows
notes.html:
References

Instructor: re-asking and validation · Anthropic: structured outputs · OpenAI: structured outputs · Tam et al. 2024: Let Me Speak Freely?

TL;DR

When an output fails, send the model its own output and the exact error, and ask again. That works because the model now knows something it didn't. Sending the same request again does not. The engineering is the policy: which failures are worth another try, how many, within how much time, and what happens when you stop. The worst design is silent repair: it turns a failure rate you could watch into a quality drift you can't.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:responsestop reasonfail, never retry
raise the limit, try once moreparse + validatere-ask with the error (max 2, inside a time budget)marked failure + review queue

Recall

Prompt Answer
Re-ask vs retry? A re-ask includes the failed output and its error; a retry is the same request again.
Which failures are never retried? Refusals and policy blocks.
What must change on a cut-off? Something: a larger token limit or a smaller request.
The two bounds on a ladder? Attempts and wall-clock time.
What does the last rung return? A marked failure with the raw response kept; never a default value.
Draw by hand: the ladder Stop reason → classify → re-ask with error → change a variable → visible fallback; a counter on every rung.

The idea

An extraction service wraps its call in "try three times". At temperature zero the three attempts are the same request and return the same invalid object. Raise the temperature and it sometimes works by luck, which looks like the loop doing its job.

A retry changes nothing about what the model knows. A re-ask does: append the failed output and the validator's message, "total was −40; it must be between 0 and the order total", and ask again. The model now sees what was wrong. Errors of that local kind, a missing field, a bad enum, a number out of range, usually clear in one more attempt.

Not every failure is of that kind, so sort them first. A refusal must not be re-asked at all. A cut-off will cut off again unless you change the limit. A context overflow will overflow again. "This quote isn't in the document" is hard for the model to fix because the error doesn't say where a real quote is.

Then decide where it ends. A system of record should never receive a value the loop invented to keep things moving. The last rung is an explicit, counted failure that a person can see.

The ladder is code and always runs. Its only request is the re-ask itself.

The trade: each rung rescues some requests and costs a round trip; unbounded or uncounted, the ladder becomes the cost problem and hides the quality problem.

How it works

The ladder. Every arrow that leaves the happy path increments a counter named for its cause.

Only the purple box asks the model for anything; the rest is decided by your code.

Failure class How you recognise it Policy Why
Shape violation parser or schema error re-ask with the error, at most twice local; clears quickly
Cut-off stop reason is the token limit raise the limit or narrow the request, once the same request cuts off the same way
Meaning violation your validator re-ask once, then fall back the model may lack the missing fact
Refusal stop reason is a refusal never retry re-asking is adversarial and fails anyway
Deterministic context overflow; schema over a provider limit fail at once the outcome is certain

What the ladder costs, for a first-attempt failure rate p and a re-ask that fixes a share c of failures:

E[calls] = 1 + p + p·(1 − c) + …        ← each further rung is paid only by requests still failing
p = 0.08, c = 0.9  →  ≈ 1.09 calls       ← cheap: most repairs take one extra call
p = 0.40, c = 0.3  →  ≈ 1.68 calls       ← two re-asks on a large share: the ladder is now the cost problem

Evolution

Lineage:2020–22 regular expressions and "try again"2023 libraries that feed the validation error backAug 2024 schema enforcement removes most shape failures2024–25 refusals and incomplete outputs reported as explicit stop reasonstoday the ladder handles what enforcement can't: cut-offs, refusals, meaning
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Schema enforcement and stronger models shrink the first rungs. What won't change: some outputs will be cut off, refused or wrong in meaning, and something has to decide what happens to them.
  • Checked on: stop reasons as documented by Anthropic and OpenAI on 11 Oct 2026; the names differ per provider.

Code

A typed, bounded ladder.

def extract(doc, client, max_attempts=3, budget_s=20.0):
    msgs, deadline, limit = [user(doc)], time.monotonic() + budget_s, 2048
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        if time.monotonic() > deadline: break                     # ① wall clock, not only attempts
        r = client.parse(msgs, output_format=Invoice, max_tokens=limit)
        if r.stop_reason == "refusal":                            # ② never re-ask a refusal
            metrics.incr("fail.refusal"); return Failed("refusal", r.raw)
        if r.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
            limit *= 2                                            # ③ change a variable
            metrics.incr("repair.cut_off"); continue
        try:
            out = validate(r.parsed_output, doc)                  # ranges, quotes present, sums
            metrics.incr("ok", attempts=attempt + 1); return out
        except ValidationError as e:
            metrics.incr("repair.validation", rule=e.rule)        # ④ count by cause
            msgs += [assistant(r.raw), user(f"That failed validation: {e}. Return the corrected object.")]
    metrics.incr("fail.exhausted")
    return Failed("exhausted", r.raw)                             # ⑤ explicit, raw kept; never a default

Break it: the belief that retrying is the same as re-asking.

def scripted_model(messages):                       # stands in for a model at temperature 0
    told = any("must be >= 0" in m for m in messages)
    return {"total": 40.0} if told else {"total": -40.0}

def run(feed_error, attempts=3):
    msgs = ["extract the invoice"]
    for n in range(1, attempts + 1):
        out = scripted_model(msgs)
        if out["total"] >= 0: return f"ok after {n}"
        if feed_error: msgs.append("total was negative; it must be >= 0")
    return "still failing"
print(run(feed_error=False), "|", run(feed_error=True))
# look for: the plain retry never succeeds; the re-ask succeeds on attempt 2
# naive belief predicts: both succeed eventually

Run on Python 3.9, it prints still failing | ok after 2. The scripted model is deterministic, as a real one is at temperature zero: the same input gives the same wrong output until the input changes.

Measure it

  • Offline: on recorded failures, the share fixed by one re-ask, per failure class. A class that rarely converges should skip the re-ask and go straight to the fallback.
  • In production: repair rate split by cause and route; fallback rate into the review queue; latency at the 99th percentile for repaired requests. A rising repair rate with flat user-visible errors is the earliest warning you will get.
  • Enforced by: the ladder: bounds, classes, the breaker and the fallback are code. The re-ask's content is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: A repair loop catches a failed output, feeds the validation error back and re-asks. It works because the model gets information it lacked, so a re-ask is not a resample. The engineering is the policy: which failures are worth retrying, how many times, under what latency budget, and what happens when the budget runs out. The trap is silent repair, which turns a metric into invisible drift.

Q · Mechanism — What makes a re-ask different from a retry? A retry resamples from the same distribution: identical at temperature zero, a lottery above it. Nothing changed in what the model knows. A re-ask appends the failed output and the specific validation error, so the next attempt is conditioned on "you produced this, and it failed because the total was negative". That predicts convergence: local errors clear in one attempt; errors where the model lacks a fact, like a quote that isn't in the document, mostly don't.

Q · Trade-off — When do you retry and when do you fail fast? The simpler rung is no loop at all: with schema enforcement and a strict consumer, failing fast is a legitimate design. Where I do repair, I classify first. Shape and range errors: re-ask, twice at most. Cut-offs: once, with a larger limit. Deterministic failures: fail immediately. Refusals: never. Each retry adds a full round trip, so the ladder is bounded by wall-clock time as well as attempts, and every rung has its own counter.

Q · Failure — Repair rate is 8% and rising; user-facing errors are flat. Is that fine? No. The ladder is absorbing a degradation and converting it into latency and spend. Something upstream changed: a model update, longer inputs, a prompt edit. I'd split the repair rate by cause and route: more cut-offs point to input length, more shape errors to a model or prompt change, more meaning errors to content drift. And I'd add a breaker: above a threshold, stop repairing and fail fast, because during a provider incident repairs multiply load on the thing that is struggling.

Q · Design — The output layer for high-volume extraction feeding a system of record. A system of record must never receive a silently defaulted value, so the goal is visible failure at bounded cost. Schema enforcement first, so most shape failures never occur. Then classification by stop reason and validator rule; a re-ask capped at two; an escalation that changes a variable, a larger limit or a stronger model; and a fallback that writes a record marked as failed, with the raw response, to a review queue. A breaker and a time budget sit over all of it. The platform view is reliability engineering.

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: a re-ask vs a retry
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both call the model again after a failure.
    ↳ Difference: a retry sends the same input and can only succeed by chance. A re-ask adds the failed output and the error, so the model has something new to act on.
    ↳ Think instead: if the second request doesn't contain the error, it is a retry.
  • "With schema enforcement on, a repair loop is redundant"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: malformed output was the reason the loop was built.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: refusals and cut-offs return something that isn't your object, and wrong values pass every shape check.
    ↳ Think instead: enforcement shrinks what the ladder handles; it doesn't remove the ladder.
  • "A forgiving parser that repairs common malformations is good defence"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the pipeline keeps running and the dashboards stay green.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: that is how a regression hides. Mine absorbed a growing share of responses after a model update; the fix was a counter on every repair and an alert on the rate.
    ↳ Think instead: repair loudly: every fix counted, by cause.
  • "More retries means a higher success rate"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: each attempt is another chance.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: convergence depends on the class. Local errors clear in one attempt; where the model lacks the fact, attempts three to five are spend and latency on requests bound for the fallback.
    ↳ Think instead: cap at two re-asks and send the rest to a person.
  • Don't re-ask a refusal.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is one more failure class in the same loop.
    ↳ What goes wrong: pressing a model to answer what it declined is adversarial, rarely works and reads badly in an audit.
    ↳ Do instead: fail at once, keep the raw response, and route the case to review.
  • Don't fill a default when the ladder runs out.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a complete object keeps downstream code simple.
    ↳ What goes wrong: consumers can't tell an invented value from a real one.
    ↳ Do instead: return a marked failure and let the consumer handle its absence.
  • Shelf life: classify, feed the error back, bound, count, fail visibly: all durable. Stop-reason names and what enforcement already prevents are provider facts.

Connections

Path:JSON mode and schemasparsing and repair loopsreliability engineeringdegradation and fallback
  • Builds on a layered contract: this is the policy layer.
  • Owned elsewhere: tool error handling (Agentic) covers the same loop when the failure is a tool call inside an agent.
  • Contrasts with self-refine loops: there the model critiques itself; here code supplies the error.
  • Measured by observability: counters per rung and cause.
  • Costed in latency budget: a round trip per rung.
  • Drilled in JSON mode, schema or repair.

notes.title: Output Length & Verbosity Control — A Token Cap Is a Cut, Not a Request
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: prompting best practices · Anthropic: structured outputs

TL;DR

Three levers do three jobs. max_tokens stops generation; the model does not plan towards it. A stop sequence ends output at a literal string. Only an instruction, with a number in it, changes how long the model intends to write.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
max_tokens A hard cut, mid-sentence or mid-object. Not a length instruction.
Stop sequence Ends output at a literal string; breaks if that string can occur in content.
What shapes length A countable limit in the prompt, plus an example of that length.

The idea

A summary keeps running long, so someone lowers max_tokens from 1,000 to 150. The summaries now end mid-sentence. With schema-enforced output the same change returns half an object and the guarantee is gone.

Lever What it does Enforced? Use it for
Instruction ("at most three sentences") changes what the model plans to write no: a request the length you want
max_tokens cuts at N tokens yes, by the server a safety ceiling, set well above the target
Stop sequence cuts at a string yes, by the server delimited formats you control

Set the ceiling as a net and read the stop reason: a response that ended at the limit is a failure to handle, as in parsing and repair loops. On models that think before answering, thinking tokens count inside max_tokens, so a low cap can cut the answer before it starts.

Evolution

Lineage:completion APIs with max_tokens and stop sequences2025–26 thinking tokens share the output cap; providers add effort settings. 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).

notes.title: Prefill & Assistant-Turn Priming — What Replaced Each Use of It
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: prompting best practices (migrating away from prefilled responses) · Anthropic: structured outputs

TL;DR

Prefill, writing the first tokens of the model's reply yourself, was the strongest format lever. On newer Claude models a prefilled last turn is rejected, and each thing it was used for now has a replacement. What prefill is: system, user and prefill.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time

Recall

Prompt Answer
Status on Claude From Claude 4.6 models on, a prefilled last assistant turn returns a 400 error.
Main replacement Schema-enforced output, or a tool with an enum for labels.
Why it also cost quality A prefilled answer shape leaves the model no room to reason first.

The idea

A classifier built on a {"label": " prefill fails on every request after a model upgrade. The migrations, from Anthropic's guide (read 11 Oct 2026):

Prefill was used to… Use instead
force JSON or a label structured outputs; for classification, a tool with an enum field
skip the preamble ("Here is…") an instruction ("respond directly, without preamble"), or an answer tag you extract
steer round an unnecessary refusal a clear request in the user turn
continue a cut-off response put the partial text in the user turn and ask for the continuation

Earlier Claude models still accept it. On Anthropic, prefill also cannot be combined with JSON structured output. Other providers were not checked.

Evolution

Lineage:2023 prefill as the standard way to force a format on chat modelsAug 2024 schema enforcement does the same job with a guaranteeprefilled last turns rejected from Claude 4.6 on. ⚪ Fading (Oct 2026).

notes.title: Classification & Scoring Prompts — One Token per Label, a Threshold You Fitted
notes.html:
References

OpenAI Cookbook: using logprobs · Zhao et al. 2021: Calibrate Before Use

TL;DR

For classification, make the answer one item from a closed set, enforced as an enum. Where the API exposes logprobs, read the score of each label and threshold it yourself; don't ask the model how confident it is.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why a single-token label? One score to read, one token to generate, nothing to parse.
What do logprobs give? A score per label that you can threshold, abstain on or route by.
The caveat Raw scores aren't calibrated probabilities; fit the threshold on labelled data.

The idea

A moderation prompt returns flag or ok. The product needs a third outcome: "unsure, send to a person".

① TASK     Decide whether the comment breaks the rules.         ← job
② LABELS   Answer with one letter:      A = ok, B = flag.     ← single tokens: one score each
③ CONTEXT  <rules>…</rules> <comment>{{text}}</comment>          ← data
④ OUTPUT   enum ["A", "B"], enforced                             ← closed set; read the logprob of each

Score of B above the upper threshold: flag; below the lower: pass; between: review. Fit both thresholds on a labelled set and refit after any model or prompt change. A few-shot block shifts the scores towards its most frequent and most recent label (in-context learning), so balance it. Where logprobs aren't exposed, use an enum and treat disagreement across a few samples as the "unsure" signal. Owner: logprobs.

Evolution

Lineage:2021 label scores read from completion models; calibration proposed2023 logprobs offered on chat models2024 enums enforced by schema. 🟢 Established (Oct 2026); logprob availability differs by provider and was not re-checked for this note.

notes.title: Deterministic Prompting — Temperature Zero Is Not Reproducibility
notes.html:
References

vLLM: reproducibility · vLLM: batch invariance · Sclar et al. 2023: sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design · Anthropic: structured outputs

TL;DR

Temperature zero makes the model pick the top token every time. It does not make the numbers behind that pick identical from run to run. On shared servers your request is computed alongside others, and tiny numeric differences occasionally flip a near-tie. One flipped token changes everything after it. So don't promise identical text. Promise what you can hold: the same structure, the same decision on a test set, and a full record of what was sent.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:same prompt, temperature 0batched with whatever else is in flightsums computed in a different orderscores differ in the last digitsa different tokena different continuation

Recall

Prompt Answer
Does temperature 0 give identical outputs? No. It removes sampling randomness, not numeric variation.
Where does the variation come from? Floating-point sums computed in an order that depends on the batch.
What can you guarantee? Structure (schema, enums), measured decision stability, and an audit record.

The idea

A contract-review tool runs at temperature zero. A customer submits the same contract twice and gets "approve" once and "refer" once. Engineering spends a week looking for a caching bug.

There is no bug. Temperature zero means "take the highest-scoring token". The scores are sums of many floating-point numbers, and floating-point addition gives slightly different results depending on the order of the additions. On a shared server the order depends on what else is being computed in the same batch, which depends on traffic.

Nearly always the difference is in the last digits and the same token wins. When two tokens are almost tied, the order can decide. That is the worst kind of variation: rare, tied to load, and concentrated on the inputs where the answer was marginal anyway.

So the request "same input, same output" needs translating. Usually it means one of three things: the same decision, the ability to explain a past answer, or no silent change after a deploy. Each can be delivered, and none needs identical text.

The trade: bit-for-bit reproducibility is achievable on servers you run, at a cost in throughput and a pinned model; most products need stable decisions and a record, which cost an eval set and storage.

How it works

What can be promised, and how.

Promise Can you keep it? How Cost
Identical text, hosted API no — —
Identical text, self-hosted yes a batch-invariant mode, a pinned model, a fixed seed throughput; you run the servers
The same structure yes schema-enforced output a compile per schema
The same decision measurably a golden set and a release gate on agreement maintaining the set
An explanation later yes log the whole tuple and the raw response storage
Rule What actually happens
A seed fixes sampling only It doesn't touch the numerics before the sampler, so it narrows the variation and doesn't close it.
Providers change under you Without a pinned snapshot, the model itself can change between two identical requests.

How sampling parameters work is owned by decoding and sampling. What to log is the tuple.

Evolution

Lineage:2023 seed parameters offered, described as best-effort2024 schema enforcement makes structure guaranteeable2025 batch-invariant modes in self-hosted serving
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).
  • Stronger-model test: no. This comes from arithmetic and shared serving, not from a model's weakness. What won't change: floating-point sums depend on their order, and a hosted API decides the order for you.
  • Checked on: the vLLM pages linked above were kept from the earlier version of this note and not re-read; hosted providers' seed and temperature parameters were not re-checked.

Code

Break it: the belief that the same numbers always add up to the same total, so the same token always wins.

a = (0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3            # one order of summing
b = 0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3)            # another order, same numbers
print(a == b, a, b)
logits = {"refer": 0.6, "approve": a}                 # two tokens almost tied
pick = lambda scores: max(scores, key=scores.get)     # temperature 0: take the top one (first wins a tie)
print(pick(logits), pick({**logits, "approve": b}))
# look for: False, then two different winners
# naive belief predicts: True, and the same winner twice

Run on Python 3.9, it prints False 0.6000000000000001 0.6 and then approve refer. A difference in the sixteenth digit decided the output.

Measure it

  • Offline: run each golden-set item several times and report agreement on the decision field, against the same measure for the previous release. A drop blocks the release.
  • In production: disagreement rate on repeated identical requests (many arrive naturally as retries), per model version.
  • Enforced by: the temperature and seed settings, for sampling; schema enforcement, for structure. Identical text on a hosted API is enforced by nothing.

Interview

30-second answer: Temperature zero removes sampling randomness, it picks the top token, but it doesn't make inference reproducible. Requests are batched with whatever else arrives, floating-point sums aren't associative, so the same prompt can give slightly different scores and occasionally a different token. So I stop promising identical text and guarantee structure with a schema, decision stability with a golden set, and auditability by logging everything.

Q · Mechanism — If temperature is zero, where does the variation come from? From the forward pass, not the sampler. Floating-point addition isn't associative, so summing in a different order gives a marginally different result. The order is chosen by the hardware kernels from the shapes of the tensors, and under continuous batching those shapes depend on which other requests are in flight. Usually the top token is unaffected. When two candidates are nearly tied it flips, and one early flip changes everything after it.

Q · Trade-off — A stakeholder wants "the same input always gives the same output". What do you say? The simpler rung is to find out which need is behind the request, because it is rarely identical text. Reproducible decisions: I measure agreement on a golden set and gate releases on it. Auditability: I log prompt version, model version, settings, retrieved ids and the raw response. Stability across deploys: pinned snapshots and the same gate. If they truly need bit-for-bit reproducibility, that is self-hosted serving in a batch-invariant mode, with a real cost in throughput.

Pitfalls

  • "Temperature 0 makes the model deterministic"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: zero randomness in sampling sounds like zero randomness.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it fixes the choice among scores, not the scores. Those are computed in an order that varies with the batch, so identical requests can still differ.
    ↳ Think instead: temperature 0 is "take the top token", not "the same top token every time".
  • "Different output at temperature 0 means my setup is broken"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: in ordinary software, same input and different output is a bug.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: here it is expected behaviour of batched inference. I hunted a caching bug that was summation order under varying load; the fix was changing what we promised.
    ↳ Think instead: look for it in the guarantee, not in the code.
  • Not the same: reproducible text vs a reproducible decision
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: "the same answer" covers both.
    ↳ Difference: text is thousands of token choices, any of which may flip. A decision is one field, which can be enforced as an enum and measured for agreement.
    ↳ Think instead: shrink what must be stable to the field the business depends on.
  • Don't pay for bit-exact serving without a requirement that names it.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it makes debugging and demos cleaner.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you give up throughput and provider choice for a property most products never use.
    ↳ Do instead: log the tuple, gate on decision agreement, and reserve bit-exactness for regulated or scientific cases.
  • Shelf life: the arithmetic is permanent. Which seed and reproducibility options a provider or server offers is not.
